format: live-html

---

```{webr}
#| context: setup
#| autorun: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
download.file(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datasciencedojo/datasets/master/titanic.csv",
  "titanic.csv"
)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
df <- read_csv("titanic.csv")
```

We want to run the same analysis on the class for Titanic passengers, which is indicated in `Pclass`. 
```{webr}
#| autorun: false
df %>% count(Pclass)
```

# geom_bar()
We can show this result with a bar plot, using the geom_bar() function from the ggplot2 package. 

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
ggplot(df, aes(x = Pclass)) + 
  geom_bar()
```

This plot works when we only have *one* variable we're showing. We specify that within the aes() call, which in the above code, we put as "x = Pclass". 
We can make the same plot for other variables by changing what we set x equal to. 

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
ggplot(df, aes(x = Sex)) + geom_bar()
```

## Improving Readability 
### Labels 
We can add labels to our axes and a title for our entire plot by additonally calling labs(). 

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
ggplot(df, aes(x = Pclass)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Passengers by class", 
        x = "Passenger class", 
        y = "Count") 
```

### Themes

ggplot comes with themes (you can peruse them [here](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggtheme.html)). We can make our plot follow `theme_minimal()` by adding it. 

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
ggplot(df, aes(x = Pclass)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Passengers by class", 
        x = "Passenger class", 
        y = "Count") + 
  theme_minimal()       
```

### Fill 
We can also customize the color of the bar with geom_bar. 

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
ggplot(df, aes(x = factor(Pclass))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Passengers by class", x = "Passenger class", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```
